items.title: The local ring $A_0$ of rational functions regular at $q=0$
items.statement:
Let $q$ be transcendental over $\mathbb Q$ ([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]) and let
$$A_0:=\mathbb Q[q]_{(q)}=\Big\{\frac fg\ :\ f,g\in\mathbb Q[q],\ g(0)\neq0\Big\}\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$$
be the localisation of the polynomial ring $\mathbb Q[q]$ at the prime ideal $(q)$ ([[def-localisation-at-a-prime-ideal]]). By [[ex-the-local-ring-of-polynomials-at-x]] with $F=\mathbb Q$, the ring $A_0$ is exactly the ring of rational functions regular at $q=0$, it is a local ring ([[def-local-ring]]) with unique maximal ideal $qA_0$, and evaluation at $0$ induces an isomorphism $A_0/qA_0\cong\mathbb Q$. Since $\mathbb Q[q]$ is a principal ideal domain ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-pid]]) with nonzero prime ideal $(q)$, the ring $A_0$ is a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal; by the discrete valuation ring characterisations it is a discrete valuation ring with uniformiser $q/1$ ([[thm-equivalent-characterisations-of-a-dvr]], [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and in particular a principal ideal domain ([[cor-dvr-is-a-pid]], [[def-principal-ideal-domain]]), with field of fractions $\mathbb Q(q)$ ([[cor-rational-function-field-as-a-fraction-field]]).

By [[def-discrete-valuation-ring]] a discrete valuation ring is the valuation ring $V_v=\{x:v(x)\ge0\}$ of a discrete valuation $v$ on its fraction field. The discrete valuation of $\mathbb Q(q)$ with $V_v=A_0$ and $v(q)=1$ is the **$q$-adic valuation**; write it $\operatorname{ord}_q$, so that
$$\operatorname{ord}_q:\mathbb Q(q)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\cup\{\infty\},\qquad A_0=\{h\in\mathbb Q(q):\operatorname{ord}_q(h)\ge0\},\qquad \operatorname{ord}_q(q)=1 .$$
Equivalently, $\operatorname{ord}_q$ is the vanishing order at $q=0$. The units of $A_0$ are exactly the fractions $f/g$ with $f(0)\neq0$ and $g(0)\neq0$, and $qA_0$ is the maximal ideal, so $q$ is a uniformiser of $A_0$ ([[thm-localisation-at-a-prime-is-local]]).

This ring $A_0$ is the **crystal limiting ring** of the crystal development below, and it is different from the Laurent ring $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ of [[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]: $q^{-1}\in A\setminus A_0$, while $(1+q)^{-1}\in A_0\setminus A$; neither ring contains the other, and both are subrings of $\mathbb Q(q)$. For every free $A_0$-module $L$ the canonical map
$$\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L\longrightarrow L/qL,\qquad c\otimes\ell\mapsto c\,\ell+qL,$$
is an isomorphism, and for every $\lambda\in\mathbb Q(q)^\times$ one has $\lambda L/q\lambda L\cong L/qL$; passing from $L$ to $L/qL$ is the **crystal limit**. No freeness of any further module, no lattice and no choice principle is asserted here.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Evaluation at $0$ has kernel $(q)$ and induces $\mathbb Q[q]/(q)\cong\mathbb Q$, so $(q)$ is a maximal ideal of $\mathbb Q[q]$ and $q\neq0$ ([[def-local-ring]]); in particular $(q)$ is a nonzero prime ideal of the PID $\mathbb Q[q]$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 The field of fractions of $A_0$ is $\mathbb Q(q)$: every polynomial $f\in\mathbb Q[q]$ lies in $A_0$ as $f/1$, so $\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)$ contains $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb Q[q])=\mathbb Q(q)$ by [L3]; conversely $A_0\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$ and $\mathbb Q(q)$ is a field, so $\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$. [given, L3, algebra]

2.1 By [F2] applied to $\mathfrak p=(q)$, the localisation $A_0$ is a local ring with maximal ideal $(q)A_0=qA_0$, residue field $\mathbb Q$ under evaluation $f/g\mapsto f(0)/g(0)$: this map is surjective on constants and its kernel consists precisely of fractions with $f(0)=0$, namely $qA_0$, and units exactly the fractions $f/g$ with $f\notin(q)$, that is, $f(0)\neq0$ and $g(0)\neq0$. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

3.1 By step 1.1, $(q)$ is a nonzero prime ideal of the principal ideal domain $\mathbb Q[q]$, and by step 2.1 the ring $A_0$ is a local domain with maximal ideal $qA_0\neq0$. Every ideal $J$ of $A_0$ is generated by its contraction: if $f/g\in J$ with $g(0)\neq0$ then $f=g\cdot(f/g)\in J\cap\mathbb Q[q]$ and $f/g=f\cdot(1/g)\in(J\cap\mathbb Q[q])A_0$, while $J\cap\mathbb Q[q]\subseteq J$ gives the reverse inclusion, so $J=(J\cap\mathbb Q[q])A_0$. The contraction $J\cap\mathbb Q[q]$ is an ideal of the principal ideal domain $\mathbb Q[q]$, hence principal, so $J$ is principal and $A_0$ is a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal. By [L1] it is a discrete valuation ring; its maximal ideal is generated by $q/1$, so $q/1$ is a uniformiser, and by [L2] there is a discrete valuation $v$ of $\mathbb Q(q)$ with $A_0=\{h:v(h)\ge0\}$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L1, L2]

4.1 Normalisation. Every nonzero $x=f/g\in\mathbb Q(q)$ can be written uniquely as $q^nu$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ and $u\in A_0^\times$: factor the maximal powers of $q$ from the nonzero polynomials $f,g$ and subtract their exponents. For the discrete valuation $v$ of step 3.1, units have value zero because both $u$ and $u^{-1}$ lie in $A_0$, so $v(x)=nv(q)$. Surjectivity of $v$ onto $\mathbb Z$ therefore forces $v(q)=1$. Set $\operatorname{ord}_q=v$; this is the vanishing order just computed, with value group $\mathbb Z$ and valuation ring $A_0$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Uniqueness and units: if $w$ is any discrete valuation with $V_w=A_0$ and $w(q)=1$, then $w=\operatorname{ord}_q$. Indeed, for $x\in\mathbb Q(q)^\times$ one has $w(x)=0$ exactly when $x\in A_0$ and $x^{-1}\in A_0$, that is, exactly when $x\in A_0^\times$; for nonzero $x$ the element $x/q^{\operatorname{ord}_q(x)}$ lies in $A_0^\times$, so $w(x)=w(q^{\operatorname{ord}_q(x)})+0=\operatorname{ord}_q(x)$, using $w(q)=1$, additivity and $w(1)=0$. Thus $\operatorname{ord}_q$ is the unique such valuation and $A_0=\{h:\operatorname{ord}_q(h)\ge0\}$, with units $\{h\neq0:\operatorname{ord}_q(h)=0\}$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Units and comparisons with $A$: step 2.1 gives the units. For the comparisons, $q^{-1}\in A$ by [L4] with $u=q^{-1}$ in $R=\mathbb Q(q)$ but $q^{-1}\notin A_0$, because $q^{-1}=f/g$ with $g(0)\neq0$ would give $g=qf$ and hence $g(0)=0$, a contradiction; and $(1+q)^{-1}\in A_0$ because $1+q$ has value $1\neq0$ at $0$, while $(1+q)^{-1}\notin A$, because the unique homomorphism $A\to\mathbb Z$ with $q\mapsto1$ of [L4] would send $(1+q)^{-1}(1+q)=1$ to $\mathrm{ev}_1((1+q)^{-1})\cdot2=1$, forcing the integer $\mathrm{ev}_1((1+q)^{-1})=1/2$, which is impossible. [step 2.1, step 5.1, L4, algebra]

7.1 The crystal limit: let $L=\bigoplus_{j\in J}A_0e_j$ be a free $A_0$-module with the displayed basis. The residue classes $e_j+qL$ form a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $L/qL$ because $A_0/qA_0\cong\mathbb Q$ by step 2.1, and the elements $1\otimes e_j$ form a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L$; the displayed map sends the second basis to the first, so it is an isomorphism. For $\lambda\in\mathbb Q(q)^\times$, multiplication by $\lambda$ is a bijection $L\to\lambda L$ carrying $qL$ onto $q\lambda L=\lambda qL$, hence induces an $A_0$-module isomorphism $L/qL\to\lambda L/q\lambda L$. No choice principle is used: the basis of $L$ is given, and all further objects are residue projections of explicitly presented fractional ideals of $\mathbb Q[q]$. [step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

items.title: Uniqueness of the $i$-string decomposition of an integrable module
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct. Reduce each vector to a finite-dimensional rank-one module, classify its simple factors by the Casimir, split the module by the generalized eigenspaces of the Casimir, and read off injectivity, existence and uniqueness of the string expansion; all arguments are finite and choice-free.

1.1 Finite-dimensional reduction. Let $u\in M_\lambda$. Choose $N\ge0$ with $E_i^Nu=0$ and set $W:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q(q)}\{F_i^{(a)}E_i^bu:0\le b<N,\ a\ge0\}$. Then $W$ is finite-dimensional: for each of the finitely many $b<N$ the local nilpotence of $F_i$ gives an integer $A_b$ with $F_i^{A_b}E_i^bu=0$, so the span of the vectors $F_i^{(a)}E_i^bu$, $a\ge0$, is already spanned by the finitely many vectors with $a<A_b$. [given, F1]

1.2 The commutation scalar. Let $v$ be a weight vector with $E_iv=0$ and $K_iv=q_i^av$, where $a=\langle\mathrm{wt}(v),h_i\rangle$. For $b\ge1$ the formula of [F4] gives $E_iF_i^{(b)}v=F_i^{(b-1)}\Theta_{i,b}v$, and $\Theta_{i,b}$ acts on $v$ by the scalar $(q_i^{b}-q_i^{-b})^{-1}\sum_{s=0}^{b-1}(q_i^{-2s}q_i^{a}-q_i^{2s}q_i^{-a})=[a-b+1]_i$ by the finite geometric-sum identities; hence $E_iF_i^{(b)}v=[a-b+1]_iF_i^{(b-1)}v$. [F3, F4, algebra]

1.3 The Casimir. Put $\varphi(K_i):=(q_iK_i+q_i^{-1}K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})^2$ and $C:=F_iE_i+\varphi(K_i)\in A_i$. Then $C$ is central in $A_i$: from $K_iE_iK_i^{-1}=q_i^2E_i$ and $K_iF_iK_i^{-1}=q_i^{-2}F_i$ one computes $\varphi(q_i^{2}K_i)-\varphi(K_i)=(q_i^{2}K_i-q_i^{-2}K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ and hence $[\varphi(K_i),E_i]=E_i(\varphi(q_i^2K_i)-\varphi(K_i))=(K_i-K_i^{-1})E_i/(q_i-q_i^{-1})=-[F_iE_i,E_i]$, while $\varphi(q_i^{-2}K_i)-\varphi(K_i)=-(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$ gives $[\varphi(K_i),F_i]=-F_i(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})=-[F_iE_i,F_i]$; so $[C,E_i]=[C,F_i]=0$, and $C$ commutes with $K_i^{\pm1}$ visibly. Moreover $C$ acts on every weight vector $v$ with $E_iv=0$ and $K_iv=q_i^av$ by the scalar $c_a:=\varphi(q_i^a)=(q_i^{a+1}+q_i^{-a-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})^2$. [F4, algebra]

2.1 The scalars $c_a$ for $a\ge0$ are pairwise distinct: if $c_a=c_b$ with $a,b\ge0$, then $q_i^{a+1}+q_i^{-a-1}=q_i^{b+1}+q_i^{-b-1}$, that is $(q_i^{a+1}-q_i^{b+1})(1-q_i^{-(a+b+2)})=0$; as $q_i$ is transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, $q_i^m=1$ forces $m=0$, so the second factor is nonzero and $q_i^{a+1}=q_i^{b+1}$ gives $a=b$. [F3, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 $W$ is a finite-dimensional $A_i$-submodule on which $E_i$ and $F_i$ are nilpotent and $K_i$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues in $q_i^{\mathbb Z}$. Indeed $F_iF_i^{(a)}=[a+1]_iF_i^{(a+1)}$ and $K_iF_i^{(a)}K_i^{-1}=q_i^{-2a}F_i^{(a)}$ show that $F_i$ and $K_i$ preserve $W$, and for $a\ge1$ the commutation formula of [F4] gives $E_iF_i^{(a)}E_i^bu=F_i^{(a)}E_i^{b+1}u+F_i^{(a-1)}\Theta_{i,a}E_i^bu$, where $\Theta_{i,a}$ acts on the weight vector $E_i^bu$ by a scalar; for $b+1<N$ both terms lie in $W$, and for $b+1=N$ the first term is $F_i^{(a)}E_i^Nu=0$, so $E_i$ preserves $W$. Nilpotence is inherited from local nilpotence on the finite-dimensional $W$, and diagonalisability with the eigenvalue form from [F1] and [F2]. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Claims (i) and (ii). Let $0\ne v\in H_\mu$. By steps 1.1 and 2.2 applied with $N=1$, the span $W_v$ of $F_i^{(a)}v$, $a\ge0$, is a finite-dimensional module with $F_i$ nilpotent, so there is a minimal $t\ge1$ with $F_i^{(t)}v=0$, and $F_i^{(t-1)}v\ne0$. Step 1.2 gives $0=E_iF_i^{(t)}v=[a_\mu-t+1]_iF_i^{(t-1)}v$, hence $[a_\mu-t+1]_i=0$, which by [F3] means $a_\mu-t+1=0$, that is $t=a_\mu+1\ge1$. Thus $a_\mu\ge0$, and $F_i^{(n)}v\ne0$ for $0\le n\le a_\mu$ while $F_i^{(n)}v=([a_\mu+1]_i!/[n]_i!)F_i^{n-a_\mu-1}F_i^{(a_\mu+1)}v=0$ for $n>a_\mu$. As $v$ was an arbitrary nonzero element of $H_\mu$, this proves $H_\mu=0$ for $a_\mu<0$ and the injectivity and vanishing clauses for $F_i^{(n)}$ on $H_\mu$. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2]

4.1 Simple factors. Let $S$ be a simple subquotient of a finite-dimensional type-1 $A_i$-module on which $E_i$ is nilpotent. Then $S$ contains a nonzero weight vector $v$ with $E_iv=0$: choose $0\ne w\in S$, let $m\ge1$ be minimal with $E_i^mw=0$ and put $v_0:=E_i^{m-1}w\ne0$; decomposing $v_0$ into weight components and using that $E_i$ preserves weights, some nonzero weight component $v$ satisfies $E_iv=0$. With $a:=\langle\mathrm{wt}(v),h_i\rangle$, step 3.1 gives $a\ge0$, $F_i^{(a)}v\ne0$ and $F_i^{(a+1)}v=0$. The span of $v,F_iv,\dots,F_i^{(a)}v$ is a nonzero $A_i$-submodule by the formulas of steps 1.2 and 2.2 together with $[0]_i=0$, so it equals the simple module $S$; these $a+1$ vectors have distinct weights, whence $\dim S=a+1$ and $C$ acts on $S$ by the scalar $c_a$ of step 1.3. [F3, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 3.1]

5.1 Generalized-eigenspace splitting. Let $W$ be as in steps 1.1-2.2. A finite-dimensional module has a composition series: take a proper submodule of largest possible dimension, whose quotient is simple, and repeat inside that submodule; dimensions strictly decrease. Since $C$ is central, it preserves this finite filtration and acts on each simple factor by some $c_a$ from step 4.1. The product of the corresponding linear operators $(C-c_a)$ annihilates $W$, since each factor lowers the filtration by one. Its minimal polynomial therefore has only these linear factors. Applying [F5], the generalized eigenspaces $W[a]:=\ker(C-c_a)^{m}\cap W$ are $A_i$-submodules with $W=\bigoplus_aW[a]$. Every composition factor of $W[a]$ has highest label $a$: a factor of label $b\ne a$, $b\ge0$, would make $C-c_b$ non-invertible on $W[a]$, whereas $C-c_b$ is invertible on the generalized eigenspace of the distinct scalar $c_a$. [F5, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Blocks. Fix $a\ge0$ with $W[a]\ne0$ and let $r:=\dim W[a]/(a+1)$, the number of composition factors of $W[a]$ counted with multiplicity. Each factor has by step 4.1 a weight-space decomposition into one-dimensional spaces of $K_i$-eigenvalues $q_i^{a},q_i^{a-2},\dots,q_i^{-a}$; Weight multiplicities add along this filtration: a lift of an eigenvector in a quotient can be projected to its eigenspace by the finite interpolation polynomial in the diagonal operator $K_i$, so the eigenspace sequence is exact. Hence the weight space of eigenvalue $q_i^{a-2n}$ has dimension $r$ for $0\le n\le a$, and $W[a]$ has no weight of eigenvalue $q_i^{m}$ with $m>a$. In particular $k:=\dim W[a]_{a}=r$, $\dim W[a]=k(a+1)$, and $E_i$ kills the top weight space $W[a]_{a}$ because it would raise the eigenvalue to $q_i^{a+2}$. [step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 String splitting of a block. For $0\ne w\in W[a]_{a}$ and $0\le n\le a$ one has $F_i^{(n)}w\ne0$: if $F_i^{(n)}w=0$ for some minimal $n\ge1$, then $F_i^{(n-1)}w\ne0$ and step 1.2 gives $0=E_iF_i^{(n)}w=[a-n+1]_iF_i^{(n-1)}w$, forcing $n=a+1>a$ by [F3]. Hence each $N_n:=F_i^{(n)}W[a]_{a}$, $0\le n\le a$, has dimension $k$, and the $N_n$ lie in the distinct weight spaces of eigenvalues $q_i^{a-2n}$, so they are independent; their sum is $A_i$-stable because $E_iF_i^{(n)}w=[a-n+1]_iF_i^{(n-1)}w$ and $F_iF_i^{(n)}w=[n+1]_iF_i^{(n+1)}w$ for $w\in W[a]_a$; being a submodule of dimension $k(a+1)=\dim W[a]$, the sum equals $W[a]$. [F3, step 1.2, step 6.1]

8.1 Existence. Let $u\in M_\lambda$ be homogeneous and let $W$ be the finite-dimensional reduction of steps 1.1-2.2, which contains $u$ and splits as $W=\bigoplus_aW[a]=\bigoplus_a\bigoplus_{n=0}^{a}F_i^{(n)}W[a]_{a}$ by steps 5.1-7.1. All generators of $W$ have labels in $\lambda+\mathbb Z\alpha_i$; within this coset the integer $\langle\cdot,h_i\rangle$ distinguishes labels because $\langle\alpha_i,h_i\rangle=2$. Thus a summand $F_i^{(n)}W[a]_{a}$ lies in label weight $\lambda$ exactly when $a-2n=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle$, and then $W[a]_{a}\subseteq M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ with $E_i$ killing it, so it is contained in $H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$. Collecting, for each $n\ge0$, the top vectors of all blocks with $a=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle+2n$ into $u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ gives $u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n$; here $u_n\ne0$ only when $0\le n\le a=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle+2n$, which is exactly the admissibility condition $n\le\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$. For a general $u\in M_\lambda$, apply this to the finitely many nonzero homogeneous components of $u$ and add. [step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 Uniqueness. Suppose $\sum_{n=0}^{N}F_i^{(n)}u_n=0$ with $u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ admissible and $u_N\ne0$. By [F4], $E_i^{N}F_i^{(n)}$ is a finite sum of terms $F_i^{(n-t)}K_i^{m}E_i^{N-t}$ with $0\le t\le n$; for $n<N$ every $t\le n$ satisfies $N-t\ge N-n\ge1$, so each term kills $u_n$ (as $E_iu_n=0$), while for $n=N$ only $t=N$ survives and, by iterating step 1.2, $E_i^{N}F_i^{(N)}u_N=\bigl(\prod_{t=1}^{N}[a_N-t+1]_i\bigr)u_N$ with $a_N=\langle\lambda+N\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$. Admissibility gives $a_N\ge N$, so $a_N-t+1\ge1$ for $1\le t\le N$ and the product is nonzero by [F3]. Hence $0=E_i^{N}0=\bigl(\prod_{t=1}^{N}[a_N-t+1]_i\bigr)u_N$ forces $u_N=0$, a contradiction. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 8.1]

10.1 Direct sum. By step 3.1(ii) applied to $H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$, the map $F_i^{(n)}$ on $H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ is injective for $n\le\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$ and zero otherwise. Steps 8.1 and 9.1 say that every $u\in M_\lambda$ is a unique sum of vectors from the nonzero spaces $F_i^{(n)}H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$, which is exactly the statement that $M_\lambda$ is their internal direct sum. All selections in the argument were among finitely many vectors or finitely many scalars, so no choice principle is used. [step 3.1, step 8.1, step 9.1] ∎

items.title: The Kashiwara operators $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ of an integrable module
items.statement:
Let $M$ be an integrable chosen $P$-graded type-1 module ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]) and fix $i\in I$. By [[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]] every $u\in M_\lambda$ has a unique admissible decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}=\ker(E_i)\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i},$$
with $u_n=0$ whenever $n>\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$. Define the **Kashiwara operators**
$$\tilde e_i u:=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_i u:=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n .$$
Both are linear maps on $M$, shifting the label weight by $+\alpha_i$, respectively $-\alpha_i$. Along each string, $\tilde e_i$ moves $F_i^{(n)}u_n$ to $F_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ and kills the top position $n=0$, while $\tilde f_i$ moves it to $F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ and kills a string exactly at its bottom, where $n=\langle\mathrm{wt}(u_n),h_i\rangle$.

Let $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$ be the projections onto the top positions and the bottom positions of these strings:
$$p_{\mathrm{top}}u:=u_0,\qquad p_{\mathrm{bottom}}u:=\sum_{n:\,n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n)}u_n .$$
Then
$$\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i,\qquad \ker\tilde f_i=\ker F_i,\qquad \tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{top}},\qquad \tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{bottom}},$$
so $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ are inverse to each other on each existing string edge. Module homomorphisms commute with both operators, $p_{\mathrm{top}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{bottom}}$. On $\ker E_i$ one has $\tilde f_i=F_i$, and on $\ker F_i$ one has $\tilde e_i=E_i$. At interior positions the operators differ from the generators: in the rank-one module $L_i(2)$ with highest vector $v$ and $u=F_iv$, one has $F_iu=[2]_iF_i^{(2)}v$ while $\tilde f_iu=F_i^{(2)}v$, and $[2]_i\neq1$. No choice principle is used. The analogous Kashiwara operators on the negative half $U_q^-$ are the shifts of its unique $e_i'$-string decomposition ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), constructed using the skew derivation of [[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]]. Their strings have no bottom: $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}$ and $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-P_i$, where $P_i$ projects onto $\ker e_i'$; the second identity follows by subtracting the position-zero coefficient $u_0=P_iu$ from the string expansion. These string-shift operators are distinct from the skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$. No negative-half operator is used in the module verification below.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct. All operators are read off the unique string decomposition string by string.

1.1 Linearity and weights. On a string position $F_i^{(n)}u_n$ with $u_n\in H_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ put $\tilde e_i(F_i^{(n)}u_n):=F_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ for $n\ge1$ and $0$ for $n=0$, and $\tilde f_i(F_i^{(n)}u_n):=F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$. By [F2] every $u$ is a unique sum of such positions inside its decomposition, so these prescriptions define linear maps on $M$; the shifted vectors lie in $M_{\lambda+\alpha_i}$ and $M_{\lambda-\alpha_i}$ respectively, since $F_i^{(n-1)}u_n\in M_{\lambda+\alpha_i}$ and $F_i^{(n+1)}u_n\in M_{\lambda-\alpha_i}$ by [F1]. [F1, F2]

2.1 The top projection. Writing $p_{\mathrm{top}}u:=u_0$ gives a well-defined linear idempotent by [F2]. For $u=\sum_nF_i^{(n)}u_n$ one has $\tilde f_i\tilde e_iu=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n)}u_n$ by step 1.1, hence $u-\tilde f_i\tilde e_iu=u_0=p_{\mathrm{top}}u$; equivalently $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i=\mathrm{id}-p_{\mathrm{top}}$, and on each position with $n\ge1$ the composition $\tilde f_i\tilde e_i$ is the identity. [step 1.1, F2]

2.2 The bottom projection. For a nonzero coefficient $u_n$, if $n\ge\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$, then $n$ equals that length by [F1], and $F_i^{(n+1)}u_n=0$ because $F_i^{(n)}$ is zero beyond the string length; thus $\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n<\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n$, which is the admissible decomposition of $\tilde f_iu$ (its $m$-th top coefficient is $u_{m-1}$ for $m\ge1$). Applying step 1.1 to this decomposition, $\tilde e_i\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n<\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n)}u_n$, so $u-\tilde e_i\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle}F_i^{(n)}u_n=p_{\mathrm{bottom}}u$; in particular on each position that is not a bottom the composition $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i$ is the identity. [F1, step 1.1, F2]

2.3 Kernels. For $u=\sum_nF_i^{(n)}u_n$, step 1.1 gives $\tilde e_iu=0$ exactly when $u_n=0$ for all $n\ge1$, that is $u=u_0\in H_\lambda$. On the other hand [F3] gives $E_iu=\sum_{n\ge1}[a_n-n+1]_iF_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ with $a_n=\langle\lambda+n\alpha_i,h_i\rangle$; here $a_n-n+1\ge1$ for $n\le a_n$ by admissibility and the term vanishes for $n>a_n$, so $E_iu=0$ exactly when $u_n=0$ for all $n\ge1$ as well; hence $\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i$. Likewise $\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n<a_n}F_i^{(n+1)}u_n=0$ exactly when $u_n=0$ for all $n<a_n$, and $F_iu=\sum_{n<a_n}[n+1]_iF_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ vanishes exactly then because $[n+1]_i\neq0$; hence $\ker\tilde f_i=\ker F_i$. [F1, F3, step 1.1]

2.4 Agreement on the kernels. If $u\in\ker E_i$ then $u=u_0$ by [F2], so $\tilde f_iu=F_iu_0=F_iu$; if $u\in\ker F_i$ then every nonzero coefficient $u_n$ sits at a bottom, $n=a_n$, so $E_iu=\sum_{n\ge1}[a_n-n+1]_iF_i^{(n-1)}u_n=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n=\tilde e_iu$; the $n=a_n=0$ strings contribute zero to both raising operators by [F3]. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

2.5 Naturality. Let $\varphi:M\to N$ be a homomorphism of weight-graded $A_i$-modules, so $\varphi$ commutes with $E_i$, $F_i$ and $K_i$ and preserves each $H_\mu$ and each weight space. Applying $\varphi$ to the admissible decomposition of $u$ gives the admissible decomposition of $\varphi(u)$ by uniqueness [F2], because $\varphi$ commutes with divided powers; hence $\varphi\tilde e_iu=\tilde e_i\varphi(u)$, $\varphi\tilde f_iu=\tilde f_i\varphi(u)$, and the same holds for the projections. [step 1.1, F2]

3.1 Interior comparison. In $L_i(2)$ take the highest vector $v=v_0$ and $u=F_iv=[1]_iv_1$; by [F3] $F_iu=[2]_iF_i^{(2)}v$, whereas $u$ is the position-$1$ vector of the string of $v$ of length $2$, so $\tilde f_iu=F_i^{(2)}v$. Since $[2]_i=q_i+q_i^{-1}$ and $q_i$ is transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, $[2]_i\neq1$, so $\tilde f_i$ differs from $F_i$ at this interior position. [F3, step 1.1] ∎

items.title: The $i$-string decomposition of the negative half
items.statement:
Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half of the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with its skew derivations $e_i',e_i'':U_q^-\to U_q^-$ ([[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], [[def-positive-negative-and-toral-quantum-subalgebras]]), fix $i\in I$, and write $f_i^{(n)}=F_i^n/[n]_i!$ for the divided powers ([[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). Then:

(i) $e_i'$ is locally nilpotent on $U_q^-$, and the endomorphism
$$P_i:=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(m-1)/2}F_i^{(m)}e_i'^{\,m}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q(q)}(U_q^-)$$
is well defined (each sum is finite on each element) and is the projection onto $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ along $f_iU_q^-$. In particular $e_i'P_i=0$, $P_iF_i=0$, $P_i^2=P_i$, $P_iu=u$ for $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, and
$$U_q^-=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'\oplus f_iU_q^-.$$

(ii) Every $u\in U_q^-$ has a unique $i$-string decomposition
$$u=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n)}u_n,\qquad u_n\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i',\qquad u_n=0\ \text{for }n\gg0,$$
and the components are given by $u_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$.

(iii) The **Kashiwara operators on the negative half**, defined on the string decomposition by
$$\tilde e_iu:=\sum_{n\ge1}f_i^{(n-1)}u_n,\qquad \tilde f_iu:=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n+1)}u_n,$$
are $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear endomorphisms of $U_q^-$ with $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\operatorname{id}_{U_q^-}$; $\tilde e_iu=0$ if and only if $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$; $\tilde f_i$ is injective and $\tilde f_i(1)=F_i$. Both operators preserve the root grading and shift its degree by $\mp\alpha_i$, that is $\tilde e_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu+\alpha_i]$ and $\tilde f_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu-\alpha_i]$.

No choice principle is used. Here $e_i'^{\,n}$ denotes the ordinary $n$-fold power of the derivation, not its divided power. The same projector and every string coefficient preserve the $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ divided-power lattice $U_A^-$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]), as proved by the integral skew-string supplier; this does not assert that lattice's freeness.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct. The projector and its finite-sum properties are those of the integral skew-string supplier [F5]; the negative-half string decomposition, the operator identities and the grading shifts are then read off string by string, with the Gaussian identity [F4] supplying the only arithmetic input.

1.1 The $q$-boson relation. By [F2] with $j=i$ and $a_{ii}=2$, $e_i'F_i=q_i^{-2}F_ie_i'+1$; applying the Leibniz rule to $F_i^r$ and summing the geometric series gives $e_i'(F_i^r)=q_i^{-(r-1)}[r]_iF_i^{r-1}$, and dividing by $[r]_i!$ yields $e_i'F_i^{(r)}=q_i^{-(r-1)}F_i^{(r-1)}+q_i^{-2r}F_i^{(r)}e_i'$ for $r\ge1$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Iterated deletion. If $e_i'u=0$, then induction on $n$ using step 1.1 gives $(e_i')^nF_i^{(m)}u=q_i^{-nm+n(n+1)/2}F_i^{(m-n)}u$ for $0\le n\le m$, while $(e_i')^nF_i^{(m)}u=(e_i')^{n-m}u=0$ for $n>m$. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

2.2 Termination. By [F2] the derivation $e_i'$ lowers positive height by one, so for homogeneous $x\in U_q^-[-\nu]$ one has $(e_i')^nx=0$ whenever $n>\sum_j\nu_j=\operatorname{ht}(\nu)$; hence on each $x$ only finitely many terms of the sum defining $P_i$ are nonzero, and $P_i$ is a well-defined $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear endomorphism of $U_q^-$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The projection. For $u\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ and $M\ge0$, steps 2.1 and [F3] give $P_iF_i^{(M)}u=\sum_{m=0}^{M}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(m-1)/2}q_i^{-mM+m(m+1)/2}\binom{M}{m}_iF_i^{(M)}u=\bigl(\sum_{m=0}^{M}(-1)^mq_i^{-m(M-1)}\binom{M}{m}_i\bigr)F_i^{(M)}u$, which by the Gaussian identity [F4] equals $u$ for $M=0$ and $0$ for $M\ge1$. Hence $P_iF_i=0$, $P_i$ fixes $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, and $P_i$ kills $f_iU_q^-$; moreover $e_i'P_i=0$ by the cancellation of consecutive terms in $e_i'F_i^{(m)}e_i'^{\,m}$ using step 1.1, so $P_i^2=P_i$ and $P_i$ is the projection onto $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ along $f_iU_q^-$, with $U_q^-=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'\oplus f_iU_q^-$ because $u=P_iu+(u-P_iu)$ lies in the two subspaces. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, F5]

4.1 Existence of the string decomposition. Let $u\in U_q^-$. By [F5], for each $n\ge0$ the element $u_n:=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$ lies in $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ (as $e_i'P_i=0$ by step 3.1), and the sum $\sum_nf_i^{(n)}u_n$ is finite because $e_i'^{\,n}u=0$ for $n$ large by step 2.2; the operator identity $\sum_nq_i^{n(n-1)/2}f_i^{(n)}P_ie_i'^{\,n}=\mathrm{id}$ supplied by [F5] gives $u=\sum_nf_i^{(n)}u_n$. [step 2.2, step 3.1, F5]

5.1 Uniqueness and the coefficient formula. Suppose $u=\sum_mf_i^{(m)}v_m$ with $v_m\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ and $v_m=0$ for $m$ large. Applying $e_i'^{\,n}$ and then $P_i$ for fixed $n$: by step 2.1, $e_i'^{\,n}f_i^{(m)}v_m=q_i^{-nm+n(n+1)/2}f_i^{(m-n)}v_m$ for $m\ge n$ and $0$ for $m<n$, and by step 3.1, $P_if_i^{(m-n)}v_m=0$ for $m>n$ while $P_iv_n=v_n$; hence $P_ie_i'^{\,n}u=q_i^{-n(n-1)/2}v_n$, that is $v_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u=u_n$. Thus the components of step 4.1 are determined by $u$, giving uniqueness and the displayed coefficient formula. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 The Kashiwara operators. Given the unique decomposition $u=\sum_nf_i^{(n)}u_n$ of steps 4.1-5.1, the prescriptions $\tilde e_iu:=\sum_{n\ge1}f_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ and $\tilde f_iu:=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ are well-defined $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear maps by uniqueness; shifting the index shows $\tilde e_i\tilde f_iu=\sum_{n\ge0}f_i^{(n)}u_n=u$, so $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}_{U_q^-}$. [step 4.1, step 5.1]

7.1 Kernel, injectivity and value at $1$. For $u=\sum_nf_i^{(n)}u_n$ one has $\tilde e_iu=0$ exactly when $u_n=0$ for every $n\ge1$, that is $u=u_0\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$; hence $\ker\tilde e_i=\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$. If $\tilde f_iu=0$, then $\sum_nf_i^{(n+1)}u_n=0$ is a decomposition with all top coefficients $u_n$ in $\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$, so uniqueness in step 5.1 forces $u_n=0$ for all $n$, that is $u=0$; hence $\tilde f_i$ is injective. Finally $1\in\operatorname{Ker}e_i'$ has decomposition $1=f_i^{(0)}\cdot1$, so $\tilde f_i(1)=f_i^{(1)}=F_i$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1]

7.2 Root grading. Let $u\in U_q^-[-\nu]$ be homogeneous. Since $f_i^{(n)}$ raises the degree by $-n\alpha_i$, the components $u_n$ of steps 4.1-5.1 may be taken homogeneous of degree $-\nu+n\alpha_i$ (decompose $u$ and each $u_n$ into finitely many homogeneous pieces and compare degrees), so $f_i^{(n-1)}u_n$ has degree $-\nu+\alpha_i$ and $f_i^{(n+1)}u_n$ has degree $-\nu-\alpha_i$; hence $\tilde e_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu+\alpha_i]$ and $\tilde f_i(U_q^-[-\nu])\subseteq U_q^-[-\nu-\alpha_i]$. [F1, step 6.1]

8.1 Integrality and choice. By [F5] the projector $P_i$ and every coefficient $u_n=q_i^{n(n-1)/2}P_ie_i'^{\,n}u$ preserve the divided-power lattice $U_A^-$, and the shifts of step 6.1 preserve it as well; no freeness of $U_A^-$ is asserted. All constructions used unique decompositions, finite sums and the explicit operator $P_i$; no choice principle is used. [F5, step 6.1] ∎

items.title: Crystal lattices, crystal bases and their crystals
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct. The induced operators, the rank and residue counts and the negative-half refinement are read off the axioms using the crystal-limit isomorphism.

1.1 Induced operators. By (iii) the operators preserve $L$ and commute with multiplication by $A_0$, so they descend to $\mathbb Q$-linear endomorphisms of $L/qL$, which is canonically $\mathbb Q\otimes_{A_0}L$ by [F3]; by [F1] they shift the label weight by $\pm\alpha_i$, so they map $L_\mu/qL_\mu$ to $L_{\mu+\alpha_i}/qL_{\mu+\alpha_i}$ and to $L_{\mu-\alpha_i}/qL_{\mu-\alpha_i}$, and axiom (v) says that they map $B$ into $B\cup\{0\}$. [F1, F3, given]

1.2 Rank decomposition. Since $L=\bigoplus_\mu L_\mu$ with every $L_\mu$ free by (ii), $\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L=\sum_\mu\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu$, and applying $\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}-$ gives $\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}L=\bigoplus_\mu\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}L_\mu$ with each summand of dimension $\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu$ by [F3]. The isomorphism of (i) is weight graded, because $L_\mu\subseteq M_\mu$ and the target is the direct sum of the $M_\mu$; hence $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}M_\mu=\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu$ for every $\mu$. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Residue counts. The crystal limit isomorphism of [F3] is compatible with the grading, and $L/qL=\bigoplus_\mu L_\mu/qL_\mu$; by (iv) each $B_\mu$ is contained in $L_\mu/qL_\mu$ and $B=\bigsqcup_\mu B_\mu$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $L/qL$, so $B_\mu$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $L_\mu/qL_\mu$. Hence $\#B_\mu=\dim_{\mathbb Q}L_\mu/qL_\mu=\operatorname{rank}_{A_0}L_\mu=\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}M_\mu$, which is the displayed equality, and the weight function of the crystal is well defined by (iv). [F3, step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.2 The graph and the partial-inverse property. By (vi) the arrow relation $b\xrightarrow{i}b'$ is symmetric under exchanging $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$, so the crystal graph has no ambiguity: an arrow exists exactly when $\tilde f_ib=b'$, equivalently $b=\tilde e_ib'$. In a finite-dimensional piece a string may end at a bottom, where $\tilde f_ib=0$; by (v) this is allowed and no vertex is added. [given, step 1.1]

2.3 The negative half. For $U_q^-$ the same discussion applies with the root grading in place of the weight grading. By [F4] the induced endomorphisms of $L/qL$ satisfy $\bar{\tilde e}_i\bar{\tilde f}_i=\mathrm{id}$, so $\bar{\tilde f}_i$ is injective and no element of $B$ is mapped to $0$ by $\tilde f_i$; with (v) this gives $\tilde f_iB\subseteq B$, the infinite-string refinement. [F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Choice. The definitions select no bases, no complements and no representatives; the lattice, its grading and the residue basis are given data, and all statements above are computations with them, so no choice principle is used. [given] ∎

items.title: Rank-one tensor strings and their crystal limit rule
items.statement:
Let $i\in I$, write $z=q_i$, and let $V(a)$, $V(b)$ be the simple rank-one modules of nonnegative integral highest weights $a,b$ for the subalgebra generated by $E_i,F_i,K_i^{\pm1}$, with divided bases $v_j=F_i^{(j)}v_0$ $(0\le j\le a)$ and $w_k=F_i^{(k)}w_0$ $(0\le k\le b)$ ([[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]]). Consider the tensor product with the coproduct $\Delta E_i=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i$, $\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$ ([[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]), its Kashiwara operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ ([[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]]) and the $\mathbb Z$-graded $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space $V(a)\otimes V(b)$ with the tensor lattice
$$L:=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{a}\bigoplus_{k=0}^{b}A_0\,(v_j\otimes w_k)$$
over the local ring $A_0$ ([[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a crystal lattice: it is a free $A_0$-module generating $V(a)\otimes V(b)$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$, it respects the weight grading, and $\tilde e_iL\subseteq L$, $\tilde f_iL\subseteq L$.

(ii) Modulo $q$ one has, for all $0\le j\le a$, $0\le k\le b$,
$$\tilde f_i(v_j\otimes w_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j+1}\otimes w_k & \text{if } a-j>k,\\ v_j\otimes w_{k+1} & \text{if } a-j\le k,\end{cases}$$
and
$$\tilde e_i(v_j\otimes w_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j-1}\otimes w_k & \text{if } a-j\ge k,\\ v_j\otimes w_{k-1} & \text{if } a-j<k,\end{cases}$$
where terms leaving the divided-basis ranges are $0$. In particular $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$ for residues $b,b'$ of the product basis (the partial-inverse property).

(iii) The nonzero residue strings are the chains $(0,t),(1,t),\dots,(a-t,t),(a-t,t+1),\dots,(a-t,b)$, $0\le t\le\min(a,b)$, and they partition the rectangle $0\le j\le a$, $0\le k\le b$.

This is a finite, choice-free calculation, independent of the grand loop and of global integral freeness.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct. Construct the rank-one highest vectors of the tensor product by an explicit recurrence, use the $\mathbb Q$ positivity of the residue form to identify the tensor lattice, compute the residues of the divided strings and read off the crystal rule; all steps are finite and choice-free.

1.1 Divided coproduct. From $\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$ and the $q$-commutation $(K_i\otimes F_i)(F_i\otimes1)=z^{-2}(F_i\otimes1)(K_i\otimes F_i)$, expanding the $n$-th power gives $\Delta F_i^{(n)}=\sum_{s=0}^{n}z^{-s(n-s)}F_i^{(n-s)}K_i^s\otimes F_i^{(s)}$: the coefficient of $(F_i\otimes1)^{n-s}(K_i\otimes F_i)^s$ in $(\Delta F_i)^n$ is $z^{-s(n-s)}\binom{n}{s}_z$, and division by $[n]_z!$ cancels the Gaussian binomials as $[n]_z!=\binom{n}{s}_z[s]_z![n-s]_z!$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 The highest vectors. For $0\le t\le\min(a,b)$ define $c_0=1$ and $c_{l+1}=-c_lz^{b-2t+2l+2}\frac{[b-t+l+1]_z}{[a-l]_z}$ for $0\le l<t$; all denominators are nonzero since $l<t\le a$, and set $h_t:=\sum_{l=0}^{t}c_l\,v_l\otimes w_{t-l}$. Substituting $\Delta E_i$ and comparing the coefficient of $v_{l-1}\otimes w_{t-l}$ for $1\le l\le t$ gives $c_l[a-l+1]_zz^{2(t-l)-b}+c_{l-1}[b-t+l]_z$, which is zero by the recurrence; the coefficients of $v_{-1}\otimes w_t$ and $v_t\otimes w_{-1}$ vanish because those basis vectors do not exist. Hence $\Delta E_ih_t=0$, and $h_t$ has weight $a+b-2t$ since $K_i$ acts on $v_l\otimes w_{t-l}$ by $z^{a-2l}z^{b-2(t-l)}=z^{a+b-2t}$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 The norm criterion. For $x=\sum_{j,k}\alpha_{j,k}v_j\otimes w_k$ one has $B(x,x)=\sum_{j,k}\alpha_{j,k}^2d(a,j)d(b,k)$, so $x\in L$ implies $B(x,x)\in A_0$ because $d(a,j)d(b,k)\in A_0$; conversely, if $B(x,x)\in A_0$ but $x\notin L$, take the minimal $N\ge1$ with $q^Nx\in L$ and let $\overline{x}\neq0$ be its residue in $L/qL$. Then $B(q^Nx,q^Nx)=q^{2N}B(x,x)\in qA_0$, while on residues the form $\overline B$ is diagonal with all entries congruent to $1$ modulo $q$, so $\overline B(\overline x,\overline x)$ is the sum of the squares of the rational residues of the coordinates of $\overline x$, a positive rational, contradicting $\overline B(\overline x,\overline x)=0$. Hence $L=\{x:B(x,x)\in A_0\}$. [F4, F6, algebra]

2.1 Valuations. By [F4], $\operatorname{ord}_zc_{l+1}-\operatorname{ord}_zc_l=(b-2t+2l+2)+(1-(b-t+l+1))-(1-(a-l))=a-t+1$ for every $l$, so the orders telescope to $\operatorname{ord}_zc_l=l(a-t+1)>0$ for $l\ge1$, with $\operatorname{ord}_zc_0=0$; hence $c_l\in A_0$, $c_0=1$ and $c_l\in qA_0$ for $l>0$. Therefore $h_t\equiv v_0\otimes w_t\pmod{qL}$, and by [F6] $B(h_t,h_t)=\sum_lc_l^2d(a,l)d(b,t-l)\equiv d(b,t)\equiv1\pmod q$, since $d(a,l)\in1+qA_0$ and the $l>0$ terms lie in $qA_0$. [F4, F6, step 1.2]

2.2 Coefficients. Put $u_{t,n}:=F_i^{(n)}h_t$ and write $u_{t,n}=\sum_{j,k}\gamma_{j,k}\,v_j\otimes w_k$; by weight, $\gamma_{j,k}=0$ unless $j+k=t+n$. Applying $\Delta F_i^{(n)}=\sum_sz^{-s(n-s)}F_i^{(n-s)}K_i^s\otimes F_i^{(s)}$ of step 1.1 to $h_t$ and using [F1] gives the finite sum $\gamma_{j,k}=\sum_{l}c_l\,z^{-s(n-s)+s(a-2l)}\binom{j}{l}_z\binom{k}{t-l}_z$ with $s=k-t+l$, over the integers $l$ with $0\le l\le\min(t,j)$ and $0\le s\le n$ (the symmetry of the Gaussian binomials rewrites the divided-power coefficients). [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 The tensored strings lie in $L$. Let $A:=a+b-2t$ and $u_{t,n}:=F_i^{(n)}h_t$ for $0\le n\le A$. By [F5](ii), $F_i^{(n)}h_t\ne0$ for $0\le n\le A$; the span of these $A+1$ vectors is generated by $h_t$ and stable under $E_i,F_i,K_i$, so it is the simple rank-one module of highest weight $A$ by [F1], and the form restricted to it is a nonzero contravariant form, hence by [F3] a multiple of the normalized form, with factor $B(h_t,h_t)$; hence $B(u_{t,n},u_{t,n})=d(A,n)B(h_t,h_t)\in A_0$ by step 2.1 and [F4]. The norm criterion of step 1.3 therefore gives $u_{t,n}\in L$. [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, step 1.3]

4.1 Integrality of the residue. Every summand in step 2.2 is an integer Laurent series in $z$: its factors $c_l$, $[m]_z$ and $\binom{N}{R}_z$ are quotients of Laurent polynomials whose denominator factors $[m]_z$ have leading coefficient $\pm1$, so their inverses are Laurent series with integer coefficients with finitely many negative terms. Since $u_{t,n}\in L$ by step 3.1, each $\gamma_{j,k}$ lies in $A_0$; an element of $A_0$ that is also an integer Laurent series has an integer residue, and the sum of the squares of the residues is $1$ because $B(u_{t,n},u_{t,n})\equiv1\pmod q$ by step 2.1 and [F4], while the Gram entries are congruent to $1$. [step 3.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, F4, algebra]

5.1 Distinguished coefficient. If $n\le a-t$, take $(j,k)=(n,t)$. The summand with $l=0$ is $c_0z^0\binom{n}{0}_z\binom{t}{t}_z=1$; a summand with $l\ge1$ has $s=l$ and valuation $l(a-t+1)+l(a-2l)-l(n-l)-l(t-l)-l(n-l)=l(2a-2n-2t+1)+l^2\ge l+l^2>0$ by the additivity of $\operatorname{ord}_z$ in [F4] (here $a-t-n\ge0$). Hence $\gamma_{n,t}\equiv1\pmod q$. [F4, step 2.2, step 4.1]

5.2 Second distinguished coefficient. If $n\ge a-t$, take $(j,k)=(a-t,\,n-a+2t)$. The summand with $l=0$ is $z^{t(n-a+t)}\binom{n-a+2t}{t}_z$, of valuation $t(n-a+t)-t(n-a+t)=0$ and leading coefficient $1$ by [F4]; a summand with $l\ge1$ and $\binom{j}{l}_z\neq0$, so $l\le a-t$, has $s=n-a+t+l$ and valuation $l(a-t+1)-s(n-s)+s(a-2l)-l(j-l)-(t-l)(k-t+l)=l+l^2>0$, where the exponent identity uses $k-t+l=s$. Hence $\gamma_{a-t,\,n-a+2t}\equiv1\pmod q$. [F4, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The residues are the chain positions. By steps 5.1-5.2 the distinguished coefficient of $u_{t,n}$ has residue $1$. Since all residues are integers and their squares sum to $1$ by step 4.1, every other coefficient has residue $0$. Hence the residue of $u_{t,n}$ is the single basis element $v_j\otimes w_k$ with $(j,k)=(n,t)$ when $n\le a-t$ and $(j,k)=(a-t,n-a+2t)$ when $n\ge a-t$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, step 5.2]

7.1 Partition into chains. Fixing $t$ and letting $n$ run over $0,\dots,a+b-2t$, the positions of step 6.1 are $(0,t),(1,t),\dots,(a-t,t),(a-t,t+1),\dots,(a-t,b)$. These are the chains of the statement, and they partition the rectangle $0\le j\le a$, $0\le k\le b$: a cell $(j,k)$ lies on the chain of $t=\min(k,a-j)$, and then it is the position $n=j$ if $k=t$ and $n=a-t+k-t$ if $k>t$ (then $j=a-t$), which determines the position uniquely. The total number of vectors $u_{t,n}$ is $\sum_{t=0}^{\min(a,b)}(a+b-2t+1)=(a+1)(b+1)$. [step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 $A_0$-basis. The matrix expressing the family $\{u_{t,n}\}$ in the product basis reduces modulo $q$ to a permutation matrix by steps 6.1-7.1, hence has determinant congruent to $\pm1$ modulo $q$, a unit of $A_0$; the adjugate identity over $A_0$ makes the matrix invertible over $A_0$. Since $\{u_{t,n}\}\subseteq L$ by step 3.1 and both families have $(a+1)(b+1)$ members, $\{u_{t,n}\}$ is an $A_0$-basis of $L$. [step 3.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 The crystal rule. By [F5] the operators act on the strings by $\tilde e_iF_i^{(n)}h_t=F_i^{(n-1)}h_t$ and $\tilde f_iF_i^{(n)}h_t=F_i^{(n+1)}h_t$, with the endpoint terms zero; since the strings form the $A_0$-basis of $L$ by step 8.1, both operators preserve $L$ and shift the residues along the chains of step 7.1. Reading off which tensor factor changes gives the two displayed rules: along $(n,t)\mapsto(n+1,t)$ the first factor moves exactly when $a-(n)>\ t$, that is $a-j>k$, and along $(a-t,k)\mapsto(a-t,k+1)$ the second factor moves, which is the case $a-j\le k$; the $\tilde e_i$-rule is read in the reverse direction, where the first factor moves exactly when $a-j\ge k$. Terms leaving the ranges are $0$. For residues $b=v_j\otimes w_k$ and $b'$: if $a-j>k$ then $\tilde f_ib=v_{j+1}\otimes w_k$ and $a-(j+1)\ge k$, so $\tilde e_ib'=b$; if $a-j\le k$ then $\tilde f_ib=v_j\otimes w_{k+1}$ and $a-j<k+1$, so $\tilde e_ib'=b$; the converse implications follow by the same two evaluations of the displayed rules. Hence $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$. No choice is used, and neither the grand loop nor any freeness over $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ enters. [step 7.1, step 8.1, F5, algebra] ∎

items.title: The crystal graph, $\varepsilon_i$, $\varphi_i$ and the weight function
items.statement:
We also write $\langle h_i,\mu\rangle$ for the datum's integer pairing $\langle\mu,h_i\rangle$.

Let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of an integrable chosen $P$-graded type-1 module $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]) with the induced operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ on $L/qL$ ([[def-kashiwara-crystal-operators]]). For $b\in B$ write $\mathrm{wt}(b)=\mu$ when $b\in B_\mu$, and define
$$\varepsilon_i(b):=\max\{n\ge0:\tilde e_i^{\,n}b\neq0\},\qquad \varphi_i(b):=\max\{n\ge0:\tilde f_i^{\,n}b\neq0\}.$$
Then (see below) both numbers are finite and
$$\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle .$$
The top of the $i$-string through $b$ is the vertex $\tilde e_i^{\,\varepsilon_i(b)}b$, of weight $\mathrm{wt}(b)+\varepsilon_i(b)\alpha_i$; its highest rank-one integer is $\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle+2\varepsilon_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)$.

In the crystal graph of $(L,B)$ the arrows $b\to\tilde f_ib$ are the inverse raising edges: on an existing edge, $\varepsilon_i$ increases by $1$, $\varphi_i$ decreases by $1$ and the weight decreases by $\alpha_i$, and the $i$-chains of $B$ are the finite strings with $\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)+1$ vertices.

For a crystal basis of the negative half $U_q^-$ ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]) one uses the same arrows and the same finite $\varepsilon_i$, but defines the **formal** $\varphi_i:=\varepsilon_i+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}\rangle$ as an integer of the abstract root-graded crystal; it may be negative, and it is not the lowering-chain length. The actual lowering-chain length of a negative-half vertex is denoted $\ell_i^-$ and equals $+\infty$, because $\tilde f_i$ is injective there; the negative half is not asserted to be an integrable finite-string module. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct. Finiteness comes from the finite string expansion of a lift; the chain structure comes from the partial-inverse axiom; the weight formula is read off the rank-one string of a highest lift.

1.1 Finiteness. Let $b\in B$ and let $x\in L$ be a lift of $b$. By [F2] the vector $x$ is a finite sum of string positions $F_i^{(n)}u_n$; along each of the finitely many strings both $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ move one position and kill the ends, so there are integers $N,M$ with $\tilde f_i^Nx=0$ and $\tilde e_i^Mx=0$. The operators preserve $L$ and descend to the quotient, so $\tilde f_i^Nb=0$ and $\tilde e_i^Mb=0$; hence $\varepsilon_i(b)$ and $\varphi_i(b)$ are finite. [F2, given]

1.2 A highest lift. Let $b_{\mathrm{top}}:=\tilde e_i^{\varepsilon_i(b)}b$ and let $y\in L_{\mathrm{wt}(b_{\mathrm{top}})}$ be a homogeneous lift of $b_{\mathrm{top}}$. Since $\tilde e_ib_{\mathrm{top}}=0$, the element $\tilde e_iy$ lies in $qL$, hence so does $\tilde f_i\tilde e_iy$; by [F2], $h:=(\mathrm{id}-\tilde f_i\tilde e_i)(y)=y-\tilde f_i\tilde e_iy$ is a lift of $b_{\mathrm{top}}$ that lies in the image of $p_{\mathrm{top}}=\mathrm{id}-\tilde f_i\tilde e_i$, that is, in $\ker\tilde e_i=\ker E_i$; it is nonzero because its class $b_{\mathrm{top}}$ is nonzero. Thus $h$ is a nonzero $E_i$-highest vector of $M$, and its weight is $\mu:=\mathrm{wt}(b_{\mathrm{top}})=\mathrm{wt}(b)+\varepsilon_i(b)\alpha_i$ by [F2]. [F1, F2]

1.3 The negative half. For $U_q^-$ and a residue class $b$ of root degree $-\nu$, the operator $\tilde e_i$ raises the root degree by $\alpha_i$ and hence lowers the height $\operatorname{ht}(\nu)$ by one; iterating, $\tilde e_i^{\,\operatorname{ht}(\nu)+1}b=0$, so $\varepsilon_i(b)$ is finite. The operator $\tilde f_i$ is injective by [F4], so $\tilde f_i^{\,n}b\ne0$ for every $n\ge0$; the actual lowering-chain length is therefore $\ell_i^-=+\infty$. The formal quantity $\varphi_i:=\varepsilon_i+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}\rangle$ is an integer, well defined on the root-graded crystal, and along a lowering edge it changes by $+1-2=-1$: indeed $\varepsilon_i$ increases by one and $\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}\rangle$ decreases by $\langle h_i,\alpha_i\rangle=2$. It can be negative (for example $\varphi_i=0$ at the unit, and $\varphi_i=\varepsilon_i-\sum_j a_{ij}\nu_j$ at degree $-\nu=-\sum_j\nu_j\alpha_j$), and it is not the length of the lowering chain. No integrability or finite-string property of the whole negative half is used. [F4, algebra]

2.1 The component is a finite chain. By [F1] the relation $b\sim b'$ if $\tilde f_i^mb=b'$ or $\tilde f_i^mb'=b$ for some $m\ge0$ is symmetric and transitive, and each vertex has at most one $\tilde f_i$-image and at most one $\tilde f_i$-preimage in $B$; by step 1.1 every class is finite, so the component of $b$ is a finite path. It has a unique top, where $\tilde e_i$ acts by $0$, and a unique bottom, where $\tilde f_i$ acts by $0$; writing $\varepsilon_i$ and $\varphi_i$ for the distances from the top and to the bottom gives $\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)+1=\#$ of vertices of the component. [F1, step 1.1]

3.1 The chain has length $a+1$. Put $a:=\langle\mu,h_i\rangle$, so $a\ge0$ and $h\in H_\mu$. By [F3], $F_i^{(n)}h\ne0$ for $0\le n\le a$ and $F_i^{(n)}h=0$ for $n>a$, so exactly $a+1$ positions of this string are nonzero. Their classes are also nonzero: if $F_i^{(n)}h=\tilde f_i^nh\in qL$ for $n\le a$, then applying the lattice-preserving $\tilde e_i^n$ gives $h\in qL$, contradicting its nonzero top residue. Thus their classes are the vertices reached from $b_{\mathrm{top}}$ by $\tilde f_i$ (while nonzero), and by step 2.1 they are precisely the vertices of the component of $b$. Hence the component of $b$ has $a+1$ vertices. [F3, step 1.2]

4.1 The formulas. If $b$ is the position $n$ of the chain, counted from the top, then $\varepsilon_i(b)=n$ and, by step 3.1, $\varphi_i(b)=a-n$. Since $a=\langle\mu,h_i\rangle=\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle+2n$ by step 1.2, this gives $\varphi_i(b)=\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle+n=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle$, and also $\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)=a=\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle+2\varepsilon_i(b)$, which is the highest rank-one integer of the top label. [step 1.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Edges. On an existing arrow $b\to\tilde f_ib$, the position increases by one, so $\varepsilon_i$ increases by $1$ and $\varphi_i$ decreases by $1$, while the weight decreases by $\alpha_i$; conversely, $\tilde e_i$ moves one position up whenever $b$ is not the top. By step 2.1 the chain has exactly $\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)+1$ vertices. [step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Choice. The data $(L,B)$, the operators and the chain positions are given or uniquely determined; all constructions above use finite sums and the unique string decomposition, so no choice principle is used. [given] ∎

items.title: The Kashiwara lattices $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ and $\mathcal L(\infty)$ and their generating sets
items.statement:
Let $\lambda\in P^+$ and let $L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]); in this page we write $V(\lambda):=L(\lambda)$, following the notation of the crystal sources. Let $U_q^-$ be the negative half with its Kashiwara operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]), and let $A_0$ be the crystal limiting ring ([[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]]).

Define $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $V(\lambda)$ generated by all vectors $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda$ ($r\ge0$, $i_1,\dots,i_r\in I$), where for $r=0$ the vector is $v_\lambda$; and $\mathcal L(\infty)$ to be the $A_0$-submodule of $U_q^-$ generated by all $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1$ ($r\ge0$), where $\mathbf 1$ is the unit of $U_q^-$. Here $\tilde f_i$ on $V(\lambda)$ are the module Kashiwara operators and $\tilde f_i$ on $U_q^-$ are the negative-half operators. Define
$$\mathcal B(\lambda):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda+q\mathcal L(\lambda):r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)/q\mathcal L(\lambda),$$
$$\mathcal B(\infty):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}\mathbf 1+q\mathcal L(\infty):r\ge0\}\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)/q\mathcal L(\infty).$$

Then, with $\pi_\lambda:U_q^-\to V(\lambda)$, $\pi_\lambda(P)=Pv_\lambda$:

(a) $\mathcal L(\lambda)=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu$ with $\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu=\mathcal L(\lambda)\cap V(\lambda)_\mu$, and $\mathcal L(\infty)=\bigoplus_{\nu\in Q_+}\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}$ with $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}=\mathcal L(\infty)\cap U_q^-[-\nu]$; correspondingly $\mathcal B(\lambda)=\bigsqcup_\mu\mathcal B(\lambda)_\mu$ and $\mathcal B(\infty)=\bigsqcup_\nu\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\nu}$.

(b) $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)$ and $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\infty)\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)$.

(c) (Recursive spanning.) For $\alpha\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$,
$$\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\sum_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i},\qquad \mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}=\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\tilde f_i\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i}\Bigr)\setminus\{0\},$$
and the same formulas with $\mathcal L(\infty),\mathcal B(\infty)$. Each $\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ and each $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ is generated over $A_0$ by finitely many monomials of total length at most $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$, hence is a finitely generated $A_0$-module.

No basis property, scalar-extension spanning or crystal-lattice property of $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ or $\mathcal L(\infty)$ is asserted here; these are conclusions of the grand loop. The script letters avoid the collision with the simple module $L(\lambda)$. No choice principle is used. Each fixed component is torsionfree inside a field vector space and generated by finitely many words of its fixed height, so it is free over the DVR $A_0$; its full field-span is proved later. The field map $\pi_\lambda$ is surjective, but exact equality on Kashiwara monomial generators is not asserted.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct. Homogeneity gives the graded decompositions, prepending a color gives the recursive spanning and stability, and finite generation plus torsionfreeness gives freeness of the components.

1.1 Grading (a). Each generator $\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}v_\lambda$ is homogeneous of weight $\lambda-\alpha_{i_1}-\cdots-\alpha_{i_r}$, and each generator of $\mathcal L(\infty)$ is homogeneous of root degree $-\alpha_{i_1}-\cdots-\alpha_{i_r}$, by [F3]. Taking $A_0$-linear combinations and using [F2], every element of $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ lies in $\bigoplus_\mu V(\lambda)_\mu$ with only finitely many nonzero components, and its weight components lie in $\mathcal L(\lambda)$; hence $\mathcal L(\lambda)=\bigoplus_\mu\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu$ with $\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu=\mathcal L(\lambda)\cap V(\lambda)_\mu$, and similarly $\mathcal L(\infty)=\bigoplus_\nu\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\nu}$. The residue sets decompose accordingly by their definition. [F2, F3, given]

1.2 Stability (b). A generator is carried by $\tilde f_i$ to the generator with the color $i$ prepended; since $\tilde f_i$ is $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear, it commutes with $A_0$-coefficients, so $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)$ and $\tilde f_i\mathcal L(\infty)\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)$. [F1, given]

2.1 Recursive spanning (c). Let $\alpha\in Q_+\setminus\{0\}$ and let $w$ be a word of total degree $\alpha$; writing $w=\tilde f_{i_1}w'$ exhibits the class of $w$ as $\tilde f_{i_1}$ of the class of the shorter word $w'$, which is a generator of degree $\alpha-\alpha_{i_1}$. This gives $\subseteq$; the reverse inclusion holds because $\tilde f_i$ preserves $\mathcal L$ by step 1.2 and lowers the degree by $\alpha_i$. For the residue sets, a word class that is nonzero remains nonzero when shortened (if $w'\in q\mathcal L$ then $w=\tilde f_{i_1}w'\in q\mathcal L$), and the displayed union minus zero therefore equals $\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$; the same argument applies to $\mathcal B(\infty)$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, given]

3.1 Finite generation and freeness. Iterating (c) from degree $\alpha$ down to degree $0$ expresses every $\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ as the sum of the images of $A_0v_\lambda$ under the words of length exactly $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$; there are finitely many such words because $I$ is finite, and for $\alpha=0$ the component is $A_0v_\lambda$. Hence each component is finitely generated over $A_0$ by monomials of length at most $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)$. It is torsionfree because it is contained in the $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space $V(\lambda)$, respectively $U_q^-$, so [F4] makes it a free $A_0$-module. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Choice and the field map. The words are indexed by finite sequences in the finite set $I$, so no choice is needed to name the generators. The map $\pi_\lambda$ is surjective by [F5], because $U_q^-$ generates $V(\lambda)$ over $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ from $v_\lambda$; no equality between $\pi_\lambda$ and the lattice projections, and no spanning over $A_0$ of the field-spanning property, is asserted here. [F5, step 3.1]

5.1 No crystal-lattice claim yet. The statements proved above are the graded decompositions, stability, recursive spanning, finite generation and freeness of the components; whether $\mathcal B(\lambda)$ and $\mathcal B(\infty)$ are crystal bases, and whether $\mathcal L(\lambda)\otimes_{A_0}\mathbb Q(q)\to V(\lambda)$ is an isomorphism, is not asserted and is deferred to the grand loop. [given, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: Highest weight tensor maps, their adjunction and the retraction $S_{\lambda,\mu}$
items.statement:
All $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps below preserve the chosen $P$-label gradings, as required of morphisms in [[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]. The $U_q^-$-linear map $S_{\lambda,\mu}$ instead shifts labels by $-\mu$.

Let $\lambda,\mu\in P^+$ and let $V(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$, $V(\mu)$, $V(\lambda+\mu)$ be the simple integrable highest weight modules with highest weight vectors $v_\lambda,v_\mu,v_{\lambda+\mu}$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]). Equip $V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)$ with the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module structure given by the coproduct $\Delta$ of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]] ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

(i) $v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$ is a highest weight vector of weight $\lambda+\mu$, and its cyclic submodule $U_q(\mathfrak g)(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)$ is isomorphic to $V(\lambda+\mu)$.

(ii) There are unique $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps
$$\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}:V(\lambda+\mu)\to V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu),\qquad \Psi_{\lambda,\mu}:V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)\to V(\lambda+\mu)$$
with $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}(v_{\lambda+\mu})=v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$ and $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=v_{\lambda+\mu}$; they satisfy $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}\circ\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}=\operatorname{id}_{V(\lambda+\mu)}$, $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is injective with image $U_q(\mathfrak g)(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)$, $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is surjective, and $V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)=\operatorname{Im}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}\oplus\ker\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$.

(iii) Let $(\ ,\ )$ be the contravariant form on $V(\lambda)$ of [[def-contravariant-form-on-an-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module]] and similarly on $V(\mu)$; define the symmetric bilinear form on $V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)$ by $(u_1\otimes u_2,v_1\otimes v_2)=(u_1,v_1)(u_2,v_2)$. Then for all $u,v$ and all $i\in I$, $h\in P^\vee$,
$$(K_hu,v)=(u,K_hv),\qquad (E_iu,v)=(u,q_iF_iK_i^{-1}v),\qquad (F_iu,v)=(u,q_i^{-1}K_iE_iv),$$
and the maps of (ii) are adjoint: $(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}u,v)=(u,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v)$ for all $u\in V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)$, $v\in V(\lambda+\mu)$. In particular $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is an isometry onto its image.

(iv) The linear map $S_{\lambda,\mu}:V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)\to V(\lambda)$ defined by
$$S_{\lambda,\mu}(u\otimes v_\mu)=u\quad(u\in V(\lambda)),\qquad S_{\lambda,\mu}\Bigl(V(\lambda)\otimes\sum_{i\in I}F_iV(\mu)\Bigr)=0$$
is well defined, because $V(\mu)=\mathbb Q(q)v_\mu\oplus\sum_{i\in I}F_iV(\mu)$; it is $U_q^-$-linear for the left multiplication action of $U_q^-$, and $S_{\lambda,\mu}\circ\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is the unique $U_q^-$-linear surjection $V(\lambda+\mu)\to V(\lambda)$ with $v_{\lambda+\mu}\mapsto v_\lambda$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct. The tensor product is integrable with finite weight spaces; universality gives $\Phi$ and the form's adjoint gives $\Psi$; the $U_q^-$-projection $S$ is read off the root-degree decomposition.

1.1 The highest vector. By [F2], $\Delta E_i(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=E_iv_\lambda\otimes K_i^{-1}v_\mu+v_\lambda\otimes E_iv_\mu=0$ and $\Delta K_h(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=q^{\langle\lambda,h\rangle}q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle}v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$, so $v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$ is a highest weight vector of weight $\lambda+\mu$; it is nonzero. [F2, algebra]

1.2 Integrability and finite weight spaces of the tensor product. Write $A:=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}$ and $B:=1\otimes E_i$, so $\Delta E_i=A+B$ and $AB=q^{-\langle\alpha_i,d_ih_i\rangle}BA=z^{-2}BA$ with $z=q_i$; for a pure tensor $x\otimes y$ choose $N,M$ with $E_i^Nx=0$ and $E_i^My=0$ (local nilpotence of $E_i$ on $V(\lambda),V(\mu)$), then $A^N$ and $B^M$ kill $x\otimes y$, and expanding $(A+B)^{N+M}$ into $q$-commuting monomials $A^{N+M-s}B^s$ shows that every term contains either $A^N$ or $B^M$; hence $\Delta E_i$ is locally nilpotent, and the same argument with $\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$ gives local nilpotence of $\Delta F_i$. A fixed tensor weight $\nu$ is a sum $\beta+\gamma$ of weights; a fixed root degree $\alpha$ has only finitely many decompositions $\alpha=\beta+\gamma$ with $\beta,\gamma\in Q_+$ (each $\beta_i\le\alpha_i$ for the finite index set $I$), and the contributing spaces $V(\lambda)_{\lambda-\beta}\otimes V(\mu)_{\mu-\gamma}$ are finite-dimensional by [F1]; hence every tensor weight space is finite-dimensional. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 The product form is contravariant. Define $(x\otimes y,x'\otimes y'):=(x,x')(y,y')$; this is symmetric and bilinear, and for $X\in U_q(\mathfrak g)$ one has $(\Delta(X)(x\otimes y),x'\otimes y')=((x\otimes y),(\sigma\otimes\sigma)(\Delta X)(x'\otimes y'))=((x\otimes y),\Delta(\sigma X)(x'\otimes y'))$ by [F4], because $\sigma$-contravariance holds on each factor. Hence the product form is $\sigma$-contravariant for the tensor action, and the three displayed identities follow from the values of $\sigma$ on $K_h,E_i,F_i$ recalled in [F3]. [F3, F4, algebra]

1.4 Part (iv): well-definedness. By [F5], $V(\mu)=\mathbb Q(q)v_\mu\oplus\sum_iF_iV(\mu)$, so every $w\in V(\mu)$ has a unique decomposition $w=cv_\mu+w'$ with $c\in\mathbb Q(q)$ and $w'\in\sum_iF_iV(\mu)$; setting $S_{\lambda,\mu}(u\otimes w):=cu$ and extending bilinearly gives the stated well-defined linear map. [F5, algebra]

2.1 Part (i). By steps 1.1-1.2 the cyclic submodule $N:=U_q(\mathfrak g)(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)$ is an integrable cyclic highest weight module of weight $\lambda+\mu$ with highest vector $v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$, so the universality in [F1] gives a $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $V(\lambda+\mu)\to N$ with $v_{\lambda+\mu}\mapsto v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$; it is nonzero, and its kernel is a submodule of the simple module $V(\lambda+\mu)$ not containing the highest vector, hence zero. Therefore $V(\lambda+\mu)\cong N$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 Part (iv): $U_q^-$-linearity. For $w\in\sum_iF_iV(\mu)$ and any $u\in V(\lambda)$ one has $\Delta F_j(u\otimes w)=F_ju\otimes w+K_ju\otimes F_jw$ with both second factors in $\sum_iF_iV(\mu)$, so both terms are killed by $S_{\lambda,\mu}$ and $S_{\lambda,\mu}(\Delta F_j\cdot u\otimes w)=0=F_jS_{\lambda,\mu}(u\otimes w)$; for $w=v_\mu$, $\Delta F_j(u\otimes v_\mu)=F_ju\otimes v_\mu+K_ju\otimes F_jv_\mu$ has first term mapped to $F_ju$ and second term killed, so $S_{\lambda,\mu}\Delta F_j=F_jS_{\lambda,\mu}$ on $V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu)$. Since the $F_j$ generate $U_q^-$ and the actions are linear, $S_{\lambda,\mu}$ is $U_q^-$-linear. [F2, step 1.4, algebra]

3.1 Part (ii), existence and uniqueness. The same universality gives $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ with $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}(v_{\lambda+\mu})=v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$; by step 2.1 its image is exactly $N$, and $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is injective since $V(\lambda+\mu)$ is simple. It is unique because $V(\lambda+\mu)$ is generated by its highest vector. [F1, step 2.1]

3.2 Part (iv): the composite. $S_{\lambda,\mu}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is $U_q^-$-linear and sends $v_{\lambda+\mu}$ to $S_{\lambda,\mu}(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=v_\lambda$; it is surjective because $U_q^-v_\lambda=V(\lambda)$ by [F1]. Any $U_q^-$-linear map $V(\lambda+\mu)\to V(\lambda)$ with $v_{\lambda+\mu}\mapsto v_\lambda$ agrees with it on the cyclic vector and hence everywhere, since $V(\lambda+\mu)=U_q^-v_{\lambda+\mu}$; this is the asserted uniqueness. [F1, step 1.4, step 2.2]

4.1 The adjoint $\Psi$ and Part (iii). The Cartan construction is homogeneous for the chosen labels, even when toral characters coincide; hence the product form is likewise label-homogeneous. For each weight $\nu$, the form on $V(\lambda+\mu)_\nu$ is nondegenerate by [F3], and $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ maps $V(\lambda+\mu)_\nu$ injectively into the finite-dimensional space $(V(\lambda)\otimes V(\mu))_\nu$; the prescription $(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}u,v):=(u,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v)$ for $v\in V(\lambda+\mu)$ therefore defines $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ uniquely and $\mathbb Q(q)$-linearly. It is a $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map because for $X\in U_q(\mathfrak g)$, $(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}Xu,v)=(Xu,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v)=(u,\sigma(X)\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v)=(u,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}\sigma(X)v)=(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}u,\sigma(X)v)=(X\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}u,v)$. The pullback form $(v,v')\mapsto(\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v')$ is a homogeneous $\sigma$-contravariant form on $V(\lambda+\mu)$ with top norm $(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)(v_\mu,v_\mu)=1$, so by uniqueness in [F3] it equals the normalized form of $V(\lambda+\mu)$; hence $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is an isometry onto its image. Then $(\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v,v')=(\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v,\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}v')=(v,v')$ for all $v'$, so $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}=\mathrm{id}$ and $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is surjective with the stated adjunction. The endomorphism $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ is idempotent with image $\operatorname{Im}\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$ and kernel $\ker\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$, which gives the direct splitting of (ii). [F3, step 3.1, step 1.3, algebra]

5.1 Uniqueness of $\Psi$. Let $\Psi'$ be a grading-preserving $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map with $\Psi'(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=v_{\lambda+\mu}$, and let $(\Psi')^{*}$ be its adjoint defined by $((\Psi')^{*}v,u)=(v,\Psi'u)$. Then $(\Psi')^{*}$ is a module map and $((\Psi')^{*}v_{\lambda+\mu},v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)=(v_{\lambda+\mu},v_{\lambda+\mu})=1$, so $(\Psi')^{*}v_{\lambda+\mu}=v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu$ because the $(\lambda+\mu)$-weight space of the tensor product is the one-dimensional space $\mathbb Q(q)(v_\lambda\otimes v_\mu)$; by uniqueness in step 3.1, $(\Psi')^{*}=\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}$, and taking adjoints gives $\Psi'=\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$. [step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Choice. The maps are defined by universal properties (determined by the image of the highest vector) and by adjunction against nondegenerate forms on finite-dimensional spaces; no basis, complement or lift is selected, so no choice principle is used. [step 4.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎
